## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

the name of a customer, officer, chief or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'transcribing, forms, clips across siloed systems', but accuracy from the job has dropped out, and the bar is recorded against 'Finished at the desk before end of shift', a row that isn't in this list.
screens.instead: Thinking of your last report from body-cam footage, how did it go? Finished quickly, during shift / Finished during shift, but it took a lot of desk time / Finished during shift, but only by putting off other work / Finished after shift ended / Still not finished or sent back for fixes

screens.why1: The study is written and I am about to send it, so deciding who asks the questions belongs right here before people see it.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and I understand at once that an AI asks aloud on video, that people can read and type or tap instead, and that the link goes by text.
screens.why3: I can make the choice as a founder, but whether officers would answer an AI face on video or want a human asking is partly a guess, since I know them from ride-alongs and calls rather than from this format.
screens.why4: Locking and recording the preselected face works, but the record shows only that one choice, so I cannot tell whether asking in my own voice or face, which matters when cops are wary of strangers and AI, is clearly on offer.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed about officers or reports is altered, and this screen only sets how my questions are delivered.
screens.instead: Who should ask them your questions? Options: Keel's AI interviewer on video (face Keel preselects) / Me, recorded in my own face and voice -- either way, officers can read each question and type or tap, and the link comes by text message.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it is obvious why I must now settle how officers will answer.
screens.why2: The choices are clear on first read, but "Hear her," "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" run into the option text and need a second read to see they are a sample link and a status.
screens.why3: I talk to patrol officers constantly and know they are on phones between calls, often somewhere loud, so I can answer this from what I know of their shifts.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct and need no escape chip, but "Both are offered" sits oddly beside a status that makes the mixed choice wait on Daphne's recording, and the 9-in-10 figure is a loose guide to how she would cope in a patrol car or on a highway shoulder.
screens.why5: It keeps my words "patrol officers" and my pick of "Read and tap" is shown as I chose it, with nothing about the product changed.
screens.instead: How should patrol officers answer? — AI interviewer: Daphne asks each question aloud on video and they talk, type or tap (ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap: they read each question and tap, speaking or typing into any box (ready now) / Let them choose when they open the link (ready in a few minutes)

screens.why1: Having just chosen how officers answer, I see why Keel now asks who gets the link: it is the last thing to settle before the study goes out to officers I've met through departments.
screens.why2: I get the three routes on first reading, but "the Contacts page" names a page this flow has never shown me, so that option takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly how I reach officers: by name through the chiefs and departments I've been meeting, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search and one open link are distinct and cover my real routes, including posting a link to a department's own group, and my pick of named people is there.
screens.why5: My answer of sending each named person their own link is kept as I gave it, and nothing here misstates my product or the patrol officers I am studying.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / People I find with Keel (search for people here, pick a list; Keel makes a link for each one, and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post one link where the people already are; each person signs in with Google, then is interviewed).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with its deciding number beside it (Frequency: 4 answered), and the Frequency card completes it with '5 needed to call it', though the line names only one of the three short cards.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, but the tally and card lines show what is counted, how many people and the bar; it takes a second look to see why 7 people answered yet only 4 count on three cards.
screens.why_b3: The Importance and Current solution lines are word for word the beliefs I checked, the dimension names match, and the statement above them uses my own 40%-of-a-shift story about footage, forms and tools that do not talk to each other.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I am one counted answer short, but the page never says to get more answers or what the result means for the idea, so I have to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the short cards are called too few rather than given a verdict, and Prevalence is only 'Holding up' at 6 of 7, marked 'at the bar', with no claim of strength.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of your 4 beliefs have 4 counted answers and need 5, because 3 of the 7 did not fall behind on reports or were not counted, so get more officers who wrote reports this week before you judge the problem; so far, 6 of 7 fell behind, right at your bar.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so the verdict and the number that decides it are together and agree.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven people, six for me and one against, with the marker at 6 labelled as my bar, so I can see what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the job, but my belief was about shift time lost to footage and paperwork, and "fell behind on their written reports" is Keel's rewording under Keel's word "Prevalence".
screens.why_b4: It says the problem is common among these 7 and points me to the next two cards, but it tells me nothing to do about the idea or that one more no would drop me below my bar.
screens.why_b5: The claim stays with "these 7", the n is visible, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps a result exactly at the bar from being called strong.
screens.instead: Common among these 7, but exactly at your bar, so one more no would drop it below; don't lean on this alone until the next two cards show how often it happens and whether it matters.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside the number that decides it, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7 and the middle answer of 5 read at once, but I need a second look to square 'your bar · 3 of 4' with '5 needed', a ghost cell and the odd legend 'beyond, the good side short of it'.
screens.why_b3: The name Frequency and the 3 to 5 days out of 7 are recognisably my claim about officers falling behind on reports, but this belief is not among the ones listed as checked on the way in, so I can't say it is the line I approved.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is true but generic: it only implies through '5 needed' that I need one more counted officer, and it doesn't say to get that answer or what it means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: Nothing overreaches: it shows 6 answered and 4 counted, names why Sean and Luis were not counted, calls the small group 'a lean, not a call', and refuses to call the belief despite all 4 falling inside my range.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted officers fell behind on 3 to 5 days, middle answer 5, which leans your way, but you need 5 counted, so get one more officer's specific answer before relying on it.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is stated at the top with its deciding number beside it, 4 answered and 5 needed, and the So line repeats both.
screens.why_b2: The caption is clear that 8 picks come from 4 people, but "your bar · 3 of 4" sits under bars counting picks and over a strip of 8 cells (3 for, 5 against) with the marker at 3, so it takes a second look to see that the bar is about people, not picks.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in, and the problem is named in my own terms as writing up calls from body-cam footage.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to act on this, but it doesn't say what to do next, such as getting at least one more officer counted, or what the tie with short staffing means for my idea.
screens.why_b5: The screen claims nothing beyond the people who answered: 6 answered and 4 counted stay visible, Sean and Luis are shown as not counted with the reason, and the small group is called out as a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 officers counted put report writing in their two, which would reach the bar of 3, but it takes 5 counted to call it, so get at least one more officer's answer; short staffing also drew 3 picks, so watch that as the rival problem.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits at the top with its deciding number beside it, 4 against the 5 needed, and the So line repeats it, though the "4 answered" there is loose wording.
screens.why_b2: The rows and the for/against tags read at once and the bar is marked, but I need a second look to square 6 answered, 4 counted and a strip of 5 cells with an unexplained ghost, and to tell "your line" from "your bar".
screens.why_b3: The belief line is the one I checked, in my words about transcribing footage, forms and clips across separate tools, and the bar is the one I accepted.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest, but it only implies I need one more usable answer and never says to get one or what that means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered and flags the small group, but the header's "4 answered" contradicts the count line's "6 answered · 4 counted", and "a lean" sits oddly beside "nothing is settled".
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 officers answered but only 4 could be counted, and 3 of those 4 fell short of finishing at the desk; get at least one more officer's account of their last call before you lean on this.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the two agree.
screens.why_b3: The name Importance and the belief line about the five hard things and the top two are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need at least one more answer, but the screen never says that or what Kenji's staffing answer means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the people who answered: the verdict withholds a call, '1 against · 1 asked' keeps the n visible, and one quote is labelled as on its own rather than as a theme.
screens.why_b6: Kenji's line adds something I did not type, that staffing gaps and response times outrank paperwork and simple reports get done in the car, which hints my pain sits in the complex reports, but it is one voice and thin.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of the 5 needed, so get at least one more officer to answer; the one against puts short staffing and response times first and writes simple reports in the car, so ask the next officers whether the pain is only in the longer reports.

screens.why1: First question of a study about my work, and asking my department's size up front makes obvious sense as a check on whether I'm who they want.
screens.why2: Department and officers are my everyday words, and I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many sworn officers my department has, so this is easy to answer from what I know.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly for a size check, and a screener gate carries no escape chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the 10 to 200 officer range and nothing about a product or company reaches me, though it does not say sworn officers.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options, and the numbers say easily out loud, so I can hear it once and answer.

screens.why1: After checking my department size, it makes sense to ask whether reports got away from me this past week, because that's what the study seems to be about.
screens.why2: Falling behind on reports after calls is how we'd say it on patrol, and I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I know whether I had reports stacking up or stayed late to finish them in the last 7 days.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chip 'I can't recall one particular call' doesn't fit because the question is about my week rather than one call, and two escape chips are one too many.
screens.why5: It stays on getting calls written up, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question ending in 'Yes or no', so I can answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you fall behind on your written reports after calls? Yes / No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: I just said yes to falling behind on reports, so asking how many days that happened this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Short and in plain words I use on the job, and I can answer it on first read, though 'fall behind' is a little loose for a shift worker, it's clear enough.
screens.why3: I know my week and which shifts left me with reports still open, so I can count the days from memory.
screens.why4: One through seven covers every possible answer after a yes, the numbers can't overlap, and 'I can't recall' is a fair way out for a frequency count.
screens.why5: It stays on my reports after calls and nothing about a product, a company or anyone's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question, 'say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold, and the escape comes last in a few words.

screens.why1: After being asked about falling behind on reports, it makes sense to ask what part of the job I'd most want made easier, and it sets reports against the other headaches of patrol.
screens.why2: It's plain on first read, and 'run of shifts', 'calls' and 'body-cam footage' are how we talk, though we'd more likely say 'last few shifts'.
screens.why3: I deal with all of these on patrol, so I can pick one straight off from my own last few shifts.
screens.why4: Most of these are real and distinct and 'None of these' fits, but 'Getting to calls without a long wait' reads oddly because the wait is usually a stacked call queue or distance, and it isn't really a chore to make easier; 'Covering shifts with too few officers' also overlaps with it, since short staffing is what makes calls stack.
screens.why5: No product or company shows through, and the report-writing option is just one item among the others, in words I'd use myself.
screens.why6: It says well: one short question, then five short parallel options I can hold after one hearing, and a single escape at the end.
screens.instead: Think of your last few shifts on patrol. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up with required training; getting to calls when they stack up; getting ready for court dates; writing up calls from body-cam footage; or covering shifts with too few officers. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After being asked which part of the paperwork I'd most like made easier, asking how it went on my last call follows naturally, though it doesn't connect to my earlier pick.
screens.why2: "How did transcribing footage, filling in forms go?" reads like a clipped list missing its "and"; I get it on a second pass, but I'd say "reviewing body cam and writing the report," and two jobs are jammed into one question.
screens.why3: I know exactly what happened with my last report, but my last call may not have needed one, or the footage review and forms may have gone differently, so I'd sometimes have to answer for the last call I actually wrote up.
screens.why4: These are real outcomes in cop words and the escape fits, but the question asks how it went while the options say when and where it got done, and "the reports keep piling up" and "details fading" add a slant, while "no report needed" and "written at the station or on a later day I came back" have no clean home.
screens.why5: No product or company leaks to me, but "transcribing footage, filling in forms" sounds like someone else's description of my job pasted in, not how a patrol officer would say it.
screens.why6: It is one question with a spoken list, but the comma-spliced stem stumbles when heard, and the last two options are mouthfuls of sentence length that are hard to hold in a list of five.
screens.instead: Think of the last call you had to write up. When did the report get finished? In the car between calls; at the desk before end of shift; stayed past end of shift; left for the next shift; or it's still not done. Or say you can't recall.
